units: the writer lost his source of income after a plant shut down
he moved into restoring old furniture
he is writing from the place where he practices his new trade
his savings are shrinking
that decline forces him to sell his pieces sooner than planned
he is learning to haggle over prices without embarrassment
every mended object brings him new buyers
he states that dread has left him since the change
he asks the woman he writes to for a reply
text: My dear friend, I am writing from the workshop where my tools now live. When the factory closed, my livelihood vanished with it, and that loss pushed open a door I would never have leaned on alone. Waiting felt worse than starting over, so I turned to the restoration of antique furniture. Wood demands patience, and it has handed mine back to me. My savings keep thinning, which forces me to sell each piece sooner than intended, so I am learning to haggle over a price without blushing. Every chair I restore seems to deliver two further buyers, and that modest chain keeps me upright. You will ask whether I miss the steady pay. I will tell you the dread is gone, and that quiet is worth more than the security I surrendered. Write back soon. I need your voice the way glue needs a hand pressing down on it.

units: a company can run short of cash even with a full order book
the lag between takings and payments to suppliers creates the trouble
negotiating a deposit at the order eases the accounts at once
short-term credit suits only a passing shortfall
borrowing against a lasting imbalance merely hides the problem
contracting out occasional work lightens the fixed costs
the margin must be examined product by product
one line sold at a loss can swallow the profit of the others
the gap between money coming in and going out must be checked every week
text: What can a firm do when the money from its sales lands long after the suppliers have been paid? That lag drains the cash and chokes the business, even when the order book is full. Which move works fastest? Reworking the terms: a deposit taken at the order eases the bank balance straight away. Should the owner borrow, then? Short-term credit suits a passing shortfall, never a settled imbalance; used on a structural weakness, it only hides the fever. How can the fixed costs be lightened? By contracting out the occasional work instead of keeping a workshop that sits idle. And if the trouble holds? Then the margin has to be read product by product, because one line sold at a loss swallows the profit made on the rest. Which figure deserves watching? The gap between money coming in and money going out, checked weekly, not once a year.

units: a head of human resources sets out two options to the staff representative
the first option is to take on seasonal hires
the second option is to give the extra load to the crews already in place in exchange for higher pay
the representative reckons that hiring costs more in training
he reckons that the second option wears down the existing crews
the manager grants that quick dismissals would damage the reputation of the company
the representative objects that exhaustion cannot be ended like a contract
both sides settle on a middle course made of limited extra help and a bonus
a further meeting is planned before the season ends
text: The head of human resources set out his thinking to the staff representative and laid two routes before him. The first was to take on seasonal hires and absorb the rise in orders that way. The second was to hand the extra load to the crews already in place, in exchange for higher pay. The representative answered that hiring would cost far more in training, while the other route would wear down the people who were already there. The manager granted that letting workers go at the first slowdown would leave the company with an ugly name, whereas a heavy week can be put right in a week. The representative countered that exhaustion, unlike a contract, cannot simply be ended. The two of them settled on a middle course: a limited amount of extra help, along with a bonus for the longer shifts. They will meet again before the season closes.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the porter moved bales between the harbor and the storehouse
his pay depended on the weight he carried
the broker brought sellers and buyers together without touching the goods
the sworn weigher vouched for the accuracy of the scales
the money changer swapped coin brought from elsewhere and kept a share
the crier announced fresh arrivals in public
the scribe kept the record of debts
these trades have vanished or taken another name
each of these roles answered a lasting need of commerce
text: Before machines came in, trade rested on a set of callings whose names have faded away. The porter moved bales between the quay and the storehouse; his pay hung on the weight he carried, and his back deteriorated well before old age. The broker never laid a finger on the goods. He merely introduced an impatient seller to a suspicious buyer. The sworn weigher vouched for the accuracy of the scales, without whom no bargain would have held. The money changer exchanged coin brought in from elsewhere and retained a share as it passed through his hands. The crier announced fresh arrivals in the square, since nothing else made them known. The scribe, last of all, kept the record of debts, because what one man remembered rarely suited the other. Such callings have vanished or taken another name, yet each answered a need that trade has never stopped feeling.

units: at the start the owner lives on savings and waits for buyers
the first visitors look around without buying anything
a hard stretch follows in which money going out beats money coming in
half the shops close during that stretch
a group of regular buyers eventually takes shape
these regulars come back every week
word passed between neighbors then draws in new buyers
the owner ends up taking on some help
the text stresses how slow the process is and that there is no magic recipe
text: Wondering what happens to a corner shop once the doors open? At the start the owner lives on savings: rent goes out, shelves get filled, and then comes the waiting. Those early weeks bring mostly browsers, people who step in, look around and walk out without buying a thing. Then comes the rough stretch, when money leaves faster than it arrives, and that is where half the shops pull the shutters down for good. If the owner holds on, a core of regular buyers takes shape, the sort who come back every week. From that point on the neighbors carry the shop along, one telling another. In the end, if the slope eases, the owner takes on some help and can breathe again. There is nothing magic in any of it, and no recipe that spares you the effort. It is a long climb, and it wants a solid pair of legs.

units: a fire gutted a textile warehouse without injuring anyone
the rolls of cloth meant for three nearby workshops were destroyed
the workshops stopped their machines for want of material
the seamstresses paid by the piece went unpaid
a distributor canceled its seasonal order
that cancellation removed the main income of the workshops
a manager describes a week of unbroken telephone calls
the insurance covers the goods but not the lost contracts
owners in the trade now split their stock between two distant warehouses
text: A fire in a textile warehouse brought a whole supply chain to a halt, and the shock caught out everyone who had thought it solid. Nobody was hurt, but the blaze destroyed the rolls of cloth meant for three workshops nearby. With no fabric, those workshops shut their machines down; with nothing coming off the machines, they could not pay the seamstresses who earn by the piece. Further along the line, a distributor canceled its seasonal order, wiping out the main income those same workshops had counted on. A manager at one of the sites says the phone rang without a break for a week, every call bringing one more consequence. The insurer will cover the cloth, not the contracts that melted away. Owners in the trade now split their stock between two warehouses far apart, a cost they used to dismiss as waste.

units: the difficulty comes from the awkwardness of saying a sum out loud
the advice is to gather your results onto a single sheet
those results must be measured in output or in customers won
the request should be made during a quiet stretch
the evening before a deadline must be avoided
the request is put in one short sentence followed by silence
the silence must be left to the other person
if the answer is no you must ask what conditions would make agreement possible
the asker comes back on the agreed date with his notes
text: Asking for a raise is like crossing a narrow footbridge: the run-up counts as much as the handrail. Everyone knows where the trouble lies. It sits in the awkwardness that grips the voice the moment a sum has to be spoken aloud. Here is how to go about it. Gather onto a single sheet what you have achieved since you took the post, counted in output produced or in customers won. Pick a quiet stretch of the calendar, never the evening before a deadline. Put your request in one short sentence, then stop talking. The silence that follows belongs to the person across from you, so do not fill it. If the answer is no, do not argue. Ask instead what conditions would make agreement possible, and write them down with care. Come back on the day agreed, your sheet in hand. Patience is not shyness. It holds the rope taut without snapping it.

units: two neighboring employment areas reacted differently to the same industrial decline
the first drew in vast logistics warehouses
that first area shows activity restored but low wages
its workforce turns over quickly
the second area funded workshops that repair equipment
recovery there was slower but median earnings are higher
both areas received an equivalent amount of public support
the length of training explains the gap between the two models
elected officials are now studying the method they used to criticize
text: Two neighboring employment areas met the same industrial decline and came out of it in opposite states, to the plain surprise of the analysts. The first went after vast logistics warehouses. Its activity has climbed back to where it stood, but wages there are crushed and the workforce turns over quickly. The second put its money into modest workshops that repair equipment. Recovery came slower, and yet median earnings have now passed those of its neighbor. Both areas drew public support of a comparable size, which rules out any budget explanation. What separates them is the training a post demands: a sorting job is learned in a week, while mending equipment takes two seasons. So the second area keeps its workers, where the first watches them leave. The officials who once mocked that slow method are studying it now.

units: the hall rests on a slab worn down by passing traffic
the vegetable growers hold the north side with their crates stacked up
the cheese and preserve stalls run along one of the side walls
those stalls are held by families settled there for generations
the sellers of cloth and haberdashery gather under a patched glass roof
a coffee counter takes the opposite side and serves as a place to talk over prices
a central aisle wide enough for two carts runs through the building
a glazed office houses the steward who assigns the pitches and takes the fee
the sloping floor carries the wash water out to a channel outside
text: The covered market hall rests on a broad stone slab, worn smooth by the passage of carts and shoe leather. Along the north side stand the vegetable growers, their crates stacked behind them like a low wall. Down one side wall run the stalls of cheese and preserves, held by families settled there for generations. Opposite, beneath a patched glass roof, gather the sellers of cloth, thread and buttons. The far side holds a coffee counter where the traders settle up and talk over prices. A central aisle, wide enough for two carts abreast, divides these quarters and carries the buyers through. At the back, a glazed office houses the steward, who assigns the pitches and takes in the fee. The floor, laid on a gentle slope, sends the wash water out to a channel beyond the walls.

units: the working week at first had no legal limit
employers announced the ruin of the workshops if a limit came
after the limit output rose
the writer explains that rise by the cost of tiredness
the weekly day of rest was fought with the same arguments
paid periods of rest met the same opposition
none of the collapses announced at each step happened
the same arguments now serve against a shortened week
the writer grants that an old line of reasoning can stop being accurate
he demands that those who repeat a disproved forecast explain why it failed
text: Shorter hours are forever set against the survival of firms, and the quarrel gains from being put back in its own order. At the outset the working week ran on with no legal limit at all, and employers swore that any limit would ruin the workshop. The limit came, and output rose, because tiredness cost more than absence ever did. Next came the weekly day of rest, denounced in the very same terms, and after it paid rest, fought with equal heat. Every step arrived with a forecast of collapse across the board, and every forecast proved false. Now we hear those same sentences aimed at a shortened week. A word of caution: nothing promises that reasoning sound yesterday is sound still. But anyone repeating a forecast disproved three times over owes us, at the very least, an account of why it failed.
